title: Class 6 Maths Introduction to Algebra: Variables, Expressions & Patterns Explained + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 6 Maths Introduction to Algebra Explained
meta_desc: Class 6 maths introduction to algebra made simple: variables, constants, expressions and matchstick patterns, plus worked case studies and a free quiz.
excerpt: The jump from arithmetic to algebra confuses most Class 6 students because one letter suddenly stands for a whole range of numbers. Here is how the NCERT chapter actually works, with two solved case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Class 6 student what n stands for and you will often get a blank look, followed by a guess: ‘fourteen?’ That guess is the whole difficulty in one word. In arithmetic every symbol has a fixed value; in the Class 6 maths introduction to algebra chapter, a letter like n deliberately does not. It stands for any number you like — and getting comfortable with that single idea is what the entire NCERT chapter is really about. Once a child accepts that a letter can hold a range of values, matchstick patterns, formulas and word problems all fall into place.

I have taught this chapter to plenty of eleven-year-olds, and the ones who struggle are almost never bad at arithmetic. They are stuck on the shift in meaning. So before any rules, let me lay out the vocabulary the chapter leans on, then walk through two real case studies of the kind the exam now asks.

Variables and constants: the two words everything hangs on

A constant is a number whose value is fixed — 7 is 7, always. A variable is a letter that can take different values: x, y, n, l. The NCERT book uses letters for unknowns precisely because they are flexible. If a book costs ₹50 and you buy b books, the cost is 50 × b, written 50b. Here 50 is the constant, b is the variable, and the moment you decide b = 3, the expression gives you ₹150.

That is the mental move to rehearse until it is automatic: a variable is a placeholder, and substituting a number into it is called finding the value of the expression.

Turning words and patterns into expressions

The chapter builds algebraic expressions from two sources: plain word statements and geometric patterns.

From word statements

Read the sentence, name the unknown, then translate.

  • ‘Five more than a number’ → x + 5
  • ‘Seven less than a number’ → y − 7
  • ‘Three times a number’ → 3m
  • ‘A number divided into two equal parts’ → n ÷ 2

A caveat worth flagging early: ‘seven less than a number’ is y − 7, not 7 − y. Order matters, and this is the single most common slip I see in tests.

From matchstick patterns

This is the part students actually enjoy. Lay out matchsticks to make a row of triangles. One triangle takes 3 sticks; each new triangle shares a side and needs only 2 more. So for n triangles you use 2n + 1 sticks. Squares in a row follow the same logic and give 3n + 1. The pattern rule is the algebraic expression — that is the whole point the chapter is making.

Terms, coefficients and like terms

An expression such as 2n + 1 is built from terms (2n and 1) joined by + or −. In the term 2n, the number 2 is the coefficient and n is the variable. A term with no variable, like the 1, is a constant term. Terms that share the same variable — 4x and 9x — are like terms and can be combined; 4x and 4y cannot. Class 6 only introduces this idea; the heavy simplification comes in Class 7, so do not push it too far here.

Case study 1: the matchstick craft table

Meera is making a border of squares with matchsticks for a school craft display. She notices the first square needs 4 sticks, and every square after shares one side, needing 3 more.

  • Find the rule. The count is 4, 7, 10, 13… — going up by 3 each time and starting one above a multiple of 3. For n squares she needs 3n + 1 sticks.
  • Check it. For n = 1: 3(1) + 1 = 4. Correct. For n = 4: 3(4) + 1 = 13. Correct.
  • Use it. How many sticks for 20 squares? 3(20) + 1 = 61 sticks.
  • Reverse it. If Meera has 31 sticks, how many squares? Solve 3n + 1 = 31, so 3n = 30, n = 10 squares.

Notice the reverse question quietly introduces the idea of an equation — an expression set equal to a number. That is exactly how the case studies in the practice book stretch a child a little beyond plain substitution.

Case study 2: pocket money and a bus pass

Arjun gets a fixed ₹200 pocket money each month, plus ₹20 for every extra chore he does. Let c be the number of chores.

  • His monthly money is the expression 200 + 20c. The constant term 200 is what he gets regardless; 20c is the variable part.
  • In a month with 5 chores: 200 + 20(5) = 200 + 100 = ₹300.
  • If he received ₹340, how many chores? 200 + 20c = 340, so 20c = 140, c = 7 chores.

Real-context problems like this one are where algebra stops feeling like a puzzle with letters and starts feeling useful. That shift in attitude is worth more than any single mark.

A sensible order to teach it

If you are helping a child at home, resist starting with terms and coefficients. Start with the idea that a letter can be any number, then substitution, then word-to-expression, then patterns, and only then the naming of parts. The vocabulary sticks far better once the child has already been using the ideas.

Try the quiz, then the case studies

Below is a free 8-question quiz on exactly these ideas — variables, forming expressions, matchstick rules and finding values. Let your child attempt it and read the explanations for any misses. When they are ready for exam-style practice, the printable case-study e-book at the end gives chapter-wise passages with fully solved questions, so a student sees not just the answer but the reasoning.

quiz.title: Class 6 Introduction to Algebra Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on variables, forming expressions and matchstick patterns. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 6 introduction to algebra: variables, expressions and patterns

questions.q: In the expression 7x + 3, what is the coefficient of x?
questions.explanation: The coefficient is the number multiplying the variable. In 7x, that number is 7.

questions.q: Which of these is a variable?
questions.explanation: A variable is a letter that can take different values. n is the variable; the others are fixed constants.

questions.q: Write ‘six less than a number y’ as an expression.
questions.explanation: ‘Six less than y’ means you start from y and take 6 away: y − 6, not 6 − y.

questions.q: A row of n triangles made from matchsticks needs how many sticks?
questions.explanation: The first triangle uses 3 sticks and each extra triangle adds 2, giving the rule 2n + 1.

questions.q: If x = 4, what is the value of 5x + 2?
In the expression 9 + 4m, which part is the constant term?
questions.explanation: The constant term has no variable. Here that is 9; 4m is the variable term.

questions.q: A pen costs ₹15. The cost of p pens is written as:
questions.explanation: Cost is 15 rupees for each pen, so p pens cost 15 × p, written 15p.
Like terms have the same variable. 5a and 2a both use a, so they are like terms.

faq.q: What does ‘introduction to algebra’ cover in Class 6 maths?
faq.a: It introduces variables and constants, using letters to stand for unknown numbers, forming algebraic expressions from word statements and matchstick patterns, and naming the parts of an expression — terms, coefficients and constant terms. It stops short of solving complex equations, which come in later grades.

faq.q: What is the difference between a variable and a constant?
faq.a: A constant has a fixed value, like 8 or ₹50. A variable is a letter such as x or n that can take different values. When you replace the variable with a number, you can find the value of the expression.

faq.q: How do matchstick patterns connect to algebra?
faq.a: Each pattern has a rule. A row of n triangles needs 2n + 1 sticks; a row of n squares needs 3n + 1. That rule is itself an algebraic expression, which is why NCERT uses matchsticks to make the idea of a variable concrete.

faq.q: Why do students find algebra harder than arithmetic at first?
faq.a: In arithmetic every symbol has one value, but a variable can be many values at once. That shift in meaning — not the calculation — is what trips students up. Plenty of practice with substitution and word-to-expression translation fixes it quickly.
